sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Meaning of Economic Planning**: Allocation of national resources according to priority targets, moving away from pure market mechanisms to achieve equity and accelerated growth.
• **Imperative vs Indicative Planning**: **Imperative planning** (Soviet model) involves complete state control over production and distribution with mandatory targets. **Indicative planning** (French model) acts as a guideline for the private sector through incentives and policy signals without mandatory coercion.
• **Evolution in India**: India adopted a **Mixed Economy** framework, practicing directive planning for the public sector and indicative planning for the private sector, transitioning in 2015 to NITI Aayog's bottom-up cooperative federalism paradigm.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Growth rate targets versus realized growth, incremental capital-output ratio (ICOR), and sectoral contribution shifts (Agriculture to Services).

items.definition: Established in August 1952 as an apex body for decision-making and deliberations on economic planning in India, chaired by the Prime Minister and comprising all Union Cabinet Ministers and Chief Ministers of States.
A diagnostic metric that measures the additional unit of capital investment required to generate an additional unit of output. Lower ICOR signifies higher economic efficiency.

A plan in which every year the performance of the plan is assessed in terms of targets and a new plan is created for the next year based on these assessments. Introduced in India by the Janata Party government in 1978 (Sixth Plan period).

The formula approved in 1969 (and modified later) for distribution of Central assistance for State Plans among the various states in India, prioritizing population, per capita income, special problems, and tax effort.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Backward Regions & Special Category States**: Historical focus on North-Eastern states, Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand for enhanced central financial assistance (90:10 funding pattern).
• **Industrial Corridors**: DMIC (Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor), CBIC (Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor) acting as spatial planning tools to bridge regional disparities.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Regional imbalances, persistent agricultural distress, unemployment, and implementation lags in infrastructural projects.
• **Policy Interventions**: Shift from top-down Five-Year Plans to 15-year vision documents, 7-year strategy papers, and 3-year action agendas under NITI Aayog.

items.title: Mnemonic for Core Objectives of Early Plans
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'G-E-S-S' (Growth, Equity, Self-reliance, Social justice).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Growth of economy, Equity in distribution, Self-reliance in technology/food, and Social justice for marginalized sections.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Quickly identifies valid macroeconomic objectives across multiple-statement questions.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: India's planning shifted from Socialist Command (1951-1991) to Regulatory Market State (1991-2015) to Cooperative Federalism Think-Tank (2015-Present).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently poses statements claiming that India practiced pure directive planning before 1991. This is incorrect; India always maintained a mixed economy with a strong private sector, operating under indicative planning elements even during early Five-Year Plans.
Mains Value Addition: Quote NITI Aayog's transition from 'resource allocation' to 'knowledge hub and monitoring institution' when writing answers on cooperative federalism and decentralized planning.

keyTakeaways: Economic planning in India transitioned from centralized, rigid Five-Year Plans to flexible, decentralised, and indicative planning driven by NITI Aayog.
The core objectives historically balanced growth, self-reliance, modernization, and social justice, which now translate to sustainable and inclusive development goals.
Understanding the distinction between imperative and indicative planning is vital for analyzing India's post-1991 economic liberalization trajectory.
